blocks.before:
\frontchapter{Abstract}
Reducing approximate nearest-neighbour (ANN) query time requires efficient
screening and selective refinement. This thesis presents JHQ-GPU, which
implements JHQ through representation-aware execution, GPU index construction
and workload-level budget calibration. Cartesian codebook factorisation
replaces each 256-entry distance table with two 16-entry tables, preserving
the real-arithmetic represented distance while reducing table storage
eightfold. Candidate-parallel scanning, packed access and lane-cooperative
refinement complement this design. Refinement budgets are calibrated through
sampled top-$k$ agreement with a larger reference budget, without ground-truth
labels or a learned predictor.

\frontchapter{Abstract}
JHQ-GPU runs JHQ's primary/residual search on a GPU. It combines index construction, packed scanning, lane refinement and workload-level calibration. Cartesian splitting replaces 256 LUT entries with $16+16$, giving a storage ratio $32/256=1/8$ with the same real-arithmetic score. Calibration compares sampled top-$k$ IDs with a larger-budget reference, without GT or a learned predictor.

Experiments on an RTX 5090 cover six datasets. Two-group tables lead in
22/24 configurations; the largest index searches 17.78 million vectors at
20.44\,GiB resident memory. Full-pool calibration meets a $10^{-3}$ held-out
recall-loss target relative to the best tested budget in 12/12 cells, with
maximum loss 0.0006; smaller samples expose workload-dependent quality risk.
At recall 0.97 and batch 1,000, JHQ leads in three of four datasets and is
near parity with IVF-RaBitQ on arXiv. OpenAI runs use TF32; FP32 checks
retain favourable comparisons under a TF32-trained cache. At batch 8 and
the same recall, CAGRA fp32 leads on all four datasets. These results
locate the execution, quality and capacity trade-offs of GPU JHQ.

blocks.before:
Product quantisation divides a vector into $M$ coordinate subspaces and
represents each with a label into a small learned codebook \cite{pq}.
If $\widehat x_m=\mathcal C_m[z_m]$, asymmetric distance computation (ADC)
keeps the query unquantised and scores
\begin{equation}
 \|q-\widehat x\|^2=\sum_{m=0}^{M-1}\|q_m-\mathcal C_m[z_m]\|^2.
 \label{eq:2-adc}
\end{equation}
A query-specific table precomputes each subspace distance. Scanning then
uses code loads, table lookups and accumulation. The product is between
subspaces; the centroids \emph{within} a learned subcodebook need not have a
further coordinate product. This distinction determines whether Chapter 5's
exact internal table factorisation is valid.

position $p$. The intermediate subspace-major copy has byte offset

\begin{equation}
 \mathsf w[j,p]=\sum_{t=0}^{3}2^{8t}Z[4j+t,p],\qquad

\end{equation}

\begin{resultblock}
\begin{proposition}[Safe rejection by a witnessed bound]
\label{prop:5-shared-bound}
Assume fixed keys, publications backed by $c$ distinct candidates, and
reads that return either the initial sentinel or one complete published
key. Rejecting a candidate only when $K_q(x)\succ\tau$ cannot remove a
global top-$c$ candidate, irrespective of publication timing.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
A publication has a set $W_\tau$ of $c$ distinct witnesses:
\[
 \max_{x\in W_\tau}K_q(x)\preceq\tau
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad K_{(c)}\preceq\tau.
\]
Sentinel reads and minima of published keys obey the same inequality. Thus
\[
 x\in\operatorname{Top}_c(U)
 \ \Longrightarrow\ K_q(x)\preceq K_{(c)}\preceq\tau_{\rm seen}
 \ \Longrightarrow\ x\text{ is not rejected}.
\]
Stale reads only loosen the bound. Publications
made after earlier safe rejections remain valid: any $c$ retained
distinct candidates still supply $c$ witnesses, whether or not they are
the best $c$ of their group.
\end{proof}
\end{resultblock}
